profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

profiles.name: Leadership Communication
profiles.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
profiles.profile: Communication and leadership are two sides of the same coin; Quintilian, the famous Roman Professor of Rhetoric, knew this when he famously declared that the best leader is ‘the good person speaking well’. At the start of this course, the participants will be introduced the main leadership and communication models and theories. They will also read leading articles from the Harvard Business Review on leadership communication. Theories that will be explored will include transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership approaches. We will also explore the roles of gender, ethics and culture in communicative leadership positions. The module will focus on the role of emotional intelligence in communicating leadership; touching on key matters such as empathy, ethics, self-awareness and self-regulation. The course will also have a distinctive liberal arts and sciences flavour to it, analysing the leadership qualities and deficiencies of characters in prose fiction, film and drama. It is especially in the worlds created by Shakespeare, where key lessons about how to lead, and how not to lead, can be learned by the leaders of tomorrow. The course will also bring in real leaders from outside the college, from both the business and public sectors, to interact with the students on the subject matter of their own communicative leadership experiences and goals. Such interactions with entrepreneurial and industry heads may lead to spin-off internships in the following academic year.
profiles.topics: inspire teams; essential leadership; blends theory; communication; sharpen; helping

profiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
profiles.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
profiles.profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.

profiles.name: Ethics
profiles.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
profiles.profile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
profiles.topics: animal rights; future generations; climate change; historical injustice; moral reasoning virtue; reasoning virtue ethics

profiles.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
profiles.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
profiles.profile: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
profiles.topics: political philosophy; emphasises essay writing; contemporary texts; presentations; poverty; pluralism

profiles.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
profiles.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
profiles.profile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.

profiles.name: European Union Politics
profiles.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
profiles.profile: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
profiles.topics: decision making rules; outlines actors; politics; policy making; employs; responses

profiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
profiles.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
profiles.profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.

profiles.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
profiles.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
profiles.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.

profiles.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
profiles.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
profiles.profile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
profiles.topics: in ‘gossoci101 introduction to sociology’; ‘gossoci202 modern sociology’; social capital; social trust; civil sphere; civil repair in modern societies

profiles.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
profiles.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
profiles.profile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
profiles.topics: multivariate statistics; linear regression; factor analysis; ANOVA/ANCOVA; logistic regression; non-parametric tests

profiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
profiles.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
profiles.profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. profiles.name: Style & Meaning
profiles.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
profiles.profile: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
profiles.topics: linguistic choices inform; choices inform meaning; addresses power dynamics; non-fiction contexts; ideological undertones; close reading

profiles.name: Rhetoric in Action
profiles.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
profiles.profile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
profiles.topics: primary school children; local primary school; persuasive speaking; rhetorical theory; voices; public-speaking

profiles.name: Persuasive Communication
profiles.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
profiles.profile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
profiles.topics: persuasion; framing; nudging; cognitive shortcuts; ethics of persuasion; climate communication

profiles.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
profiles.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
profiles.profile: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
profiles.topics: or digitally mediated work; creative; sonic poetry; unconventional forms; poetic forms; communication

profiles.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
profiles.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
profiles.profile: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
profiles.topics: romance novels; graphic narratives; film narration; non fiction; literary; interpret

profiles.name: Life & Travel Writing
profiles.description2: Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.
profiles.profile: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts.

profiles.name: Film & Text
profiles.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
profiles.profile: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
profiles.topics: interpretive strategies; viewer participation; diverse dynamics between literary text; cultural analysis; modern sociology; visual anthropology

profiles.name: Introduction to Film & Media
profiles.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
profiles.profile: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
profiles.topics: analyze how films work; technologies shape perception; covers film storytelling; cultural production; critical engagement; media

profiles.name: Media Archaeology
profiles.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
profiles.profile: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
profiles.topics: cassette tapes; early printed books; how they shaped the production; preservation of knowledge; durability influence communication; technical background required

profiles.name: From T.V. to TikTok
profiles.description2: Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.
profiles.profile: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.
profiles.topics: justin bieber performance clip; as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values; tiktok; media shape attitudes; teach fear; answers

profiles.name: Media & the Environment
profiles.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
profiles.profile: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course.
profiles.topics: animal representation; deep time; contested ideas of nature; postcolonial media; media shape environmental; environmental concerns
profiles.reviewedContent: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course.

profiles.name: Media & Race
profiles.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
profiles.profile: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.

profiles.name: The Documentary
profiles.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
profiles.profile: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
